title: Chapter 11: Money, Banking, and the Federal Reserve System
benchmark: Paul Krugman & Robin Wells, Macroeconomics (Principles SSOT, Spring 2027)

questions.title: Eliminating the Double Coincidence of Wants
questions.prompt_template: Which economic function of money directly eliminates the barter requirement known as the double coincidence of wants?

hints.text: Think about why a software engineer cannot easily trade debugging services directly for groceries.
Identify the function that allows a worker to sell labor to one party and buy goods from an unrelated party.

options_template.text: Unit of account
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Function Confusion): Serving as a unit of account standardizes price quotations, but by itself it does not settle transactions without a universally accepted payment asset.

options_template.text: Medium of exchange
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because money is widely accepted as payment for goods, services, and debts, traders no longer need to find a partner who simultaneously wants what they offer and offers what they want.

options_template.text: Store of value
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Function Confusion): Storing purchasing power over time allows saving, but many non-monetary assets like real estate also store value without solving bilateral barter.

options_template.text: Lender of last resort
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Institutional Role Confusion): Lender of last resort is a central bank stability function performed by the Federal Reserve, not one of the three economic functions of money.

questions.title: Money as a Unit of Account
questions.prompt_template: When an online retailer posts all product prices in U.S. dollars and a household compares monthly rent against its grocery budget in dollars, money is primarily functioning as a:

hints.text: Notice that no physical exchange is occurring yet—values are being quoted and compared on a common scale.
Recall the function of money that reduces N(N-1)/2 barter exchange ratios down to N standardized prices.

options_template.text: Unit of account
options_template.feedback: Correct. As a unit of account, money provides a standardized yardstick for quoting prices, recording debts, and comparing the economic value of different goods and services.

options_template.text: Medium of exchange
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Function Confusion): Medium of exchange applies when money is handed over to settle a transaction, whereas quoting and comparing prices illustrates the unit-of-account function.

options_template.text: Store of value
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Function Confusion): Store of value refers to carrying purchasing power from the present into the future, not quoting relative prices on a common scale.

options_template.text: Commodity standard
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Monetary System Confusion): A commodity standard describes what backs a currency, not one of the three core economic functions of money.

questions.title: Store of Value, Liquidity, and Inflation
questions.prompt_template: What distinguishes money from other stores of value such as real estate or corporate equities, and what is the main macroeconomic threat to money's effectiveness as a store of value?

hints.text: Compare how quickly you can spend a checking balance versus selling a house without losing nominal value.
Consider what happens to the real purchasing power of a fixed dollar amount when the overall price level rises.

options_template.text: Money earns the highest long-run real return; deflation is its main threat.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Return-Liquidity Inversion): Cash and checking accounts typically pay low or zero nominal interest, and inflation—not deflation—erodes the real purchasing power of money.

options_template.text: Money has intrinsic physical value; technological obsolescence is its main threat.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Commodity Fallacy): Modern fiat money has zero intrinsic physical value, and its purchasing power is threatened by rising general price levels rather than obsolescence.

options_template.text: Money combines value storage with immediate liquidity; inflation erodes its real purchasing power.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Money is uniquely liquid because it can be spent immediately without brokerage fees or delay, but sustained inflation reduces the quantity of goods and services each dollar can buy.

options_template.text: Money is backed by corporate earnings; bank reserve ratios are its main threat.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Asset Confusion): Corporate equities are backed by firm earnings, whereas fiat money's real value is eroded by inflation rather than reserve ratios.

questions.title: Defining Fiat Money
questions.prompt_template: Which statement accurately contrasts commodity money with fiat money?

hints.text: Ask whether gold coins and Federal Reserve notes have value outside their use as currency.
Recall what establishes the legal tender status and purchasing power of modern U.S. currency.

options_template.text: Fiat money is redeemable for a fixed weight of gold at the central bank, whereas commodity money is unbacked.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Definition Reversal): That reverses the definitions; fiat money is not redeemable for gold or silver, whereas commodity money derives value from its physical substance.

options_template.text: Commodity money is issued exclusively by central banks, whereas fiat money is issued exclusively by private merchants.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Issuer Confusion): Central banks issue modern fiat currency by government decree, whereas commodity money historically circulated as physical goods like gold, silver, or salt.

options_template.text: Fiat money eliminates all risk of inflation because governments cannot expand its supply.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Supply-Constraint Confusion): Because fiat money has no physical mining constraint, it requires disciplined central bank stewardship to prevent over-issuance and inflation.

options_template.text: Commodity money has intrinsic non-monetary value, whereas fiat money has no intrinsic value and relies on government decree and public trust.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Gold or silver coins have industrial and ornamental value outside exchange, while fiat currency functions as legal tender backed by collective trust and credible monetary policy.

questions.title: Components of Post-May 2020 M1
questions.prompt_template: Under the Federal Reserve's post-May 2020 H.6 Statistical Release, which set of items is included in the M1 monetary aggregate?

hints.text: Remember that in May 2020 the Federal Reserve reclassified household savings deposits into 'other liquid deposits.'
Check the additive identity M1 = C + DD + OLD and exclude time deposits and credit lines.

options_template.text: Currency in circulation outside banks, traveler's checks, demand deposits, and other liquid deposits (including savings deposits and NOW accounts)
options_template.feedback: Correct. Following the May 2020 H.6 revision, M1 equals currency in public circulation plus demand deposits, traveler's checks, and other liquid deposits, which include household savings accounts.

options_template.text: Currency in circulation, vault cash inside commercial banks, demand deposits, and small-denomination time deposits
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Double Counting & M2 Leakage): Vault cash is excluded from M1 to prevent double counting, and small-denomination time deposits belong in M2 rather than M1.

options_template.text: Currency in circulation, demand deposits, and unused household credit card limits
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Credit-as-Money Fallacy): Unused credit card limits represent borrowing capacity (debt), not existing money, and this choice also omits other liquid deposits.

options_template.text: Currency in circulation and demand deposits only, because savings deposits are counted exclusively in M2
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Outdated Pre-2020 Definition): Before May 2020 savings deposits were excluded from M1, but after Regulation D's transfer limit was lifted, savings deposits were moved into M1.

questions.title: Components Added to M1 to Form M2
questions.prompt_template: In the post-May 2020 Federal Reserve framework, which two categories are added to M1 to obtain the broader M2 monetary aggregate?

hints.text: Recall the equation M2 = M1 + STD + RMMF.
Distinguish retail near-money balances from institutional deposits of $100,000 or more and securities.

options_template.text: Large-denomination time deposits ($100,000 or more) and corporate bonds
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Excluded Assets Confusion): Large institutional time deposits and corporate bonds are excluded from both M1 and M2.

options_template.text: Household savings deposits and commercial bank vault cash
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Pre-2020 & Vault Cash Error): Household savings deposits are already inside post-May 2020 M1, and bank vault cash is excluded from both M1 and M2.

options_template.text: Small-denomination time deposits (under $100,000) and retail money market mutual fund shares
options_template.feedback: Correct. M2 builds directly on M1 by adding retail near-money assets: small-denomination certificates of deposit (< $100,000) and retail money market mutual fund balances.

options_template.text: Unused credit card limits and U.S. Treasury bills held by households
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Credit & Security Inclusion Error): Neither credit card lines nor marketable Treasury securities are included in M2.

questions.title: Why Credit Cards, Debit Cards, and Vault Cash Are Excluded as Separate M1 Items
questions.prompt_template: Why does the Federal Reserve exclude commercial bank vault cash from currency in circulation (C) and exclude credit card limits from both M1 and M2?

hints.text: Think about what would happen if a customer's $100 checking deposit and the $100 bill sitting in the bank's vault were both counted in M1.
Ask whether swiping a credit card transfers an existing monetary asset or creates a short-term loan.

options_template.text: Vault cash is illiquid and cannot be spent, while credit cards are already counted inside M2.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Liquidity & M2 Error): Vault cash is physical currency (excluded to prevent double counting, not because it is illiquid), and credit cards are excluded from M2 as well as M1.

options_template.text: Excluding vault cash prevents double counting dollars already represented by customer deposits, and credit card limits are lines of credit rather than money.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Counting both bank vault cash and customer checking deposits would count the same dollar twice, and swiping a credit card creates a short-term loan that must later be settled using M1 funds.

options_template.text: Vault cash belongs to the U.S. Treasury rather than commercial banks, while credit cards are counted as demand deposits.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ownership & Classification Error): Vault cash is an asset of commercial banks (part of bank reserves R), and credit cards are debt instruments rather than demand deposits.

options_template.text: Both vault cash and credit card limits are excluded solely because they are held by foreign investors.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Irrelevant Criterion): Exclusion is based on avoiding double counting and distinguishing debt instruments from monetary assets, not on investor nationality.

questions.title: Maturity Transformation by Commercial Banks
questions.prompt_template: What does economists' term 'maturity transformation' describe in commercial banking?

hints.text: Compare the time horizon of a depositor's checking account with the time horizon of a 30-year mortgage.
Focus on the mismatch between short-term bank liabilities and long-term bank assets.

options_template.text: Converting physical gold reserves into digital fiat currency at the Federal Reserve
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Monetary Regime Confusion): Modern U.S. banks operate in a fiat system and do not convert gold into currency.

options_template.text: Reclassifying savings deposits from M2 into M1 when Regulation D rules change
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Statistical Classification Confusion): Moving savings deposits into M1 was a Federal Reserve statistical revision, not maturity transformation.

options_template.text: Exchanging defaulted commercial loans for government-issued Treasury bills at face value
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Bailout Confusion): Commercial banks cannot automatically swap defaulted loans for Treasury bills; loan losses are absorbed by bank capital.

options_template.text: Funding long-term, relatively illiquid loans with short-term deposits that customers can withdraw on demand
options_template.feedback: Correct. Commercial banks borrow short (demand and savings deposits) and lend long (mortgages and multi-year business loans), creating liquidity for savers while financing long-term investment.

questions.title: Definition and Role of Bank Capital (Net Worth)
questions.prompt_template: On a commercial bank's balance sheet, how is bank capital (net worth) defined and what is its primary economic purpose?

hints.text: Recall the accounting identity Assets = Liabilities + Bank Capital.
Ask who absorbs the loss first when a borrower defaults on a bank loan.

options_template.text: Assets minus liabilities; it acts as an equity buffer that absorbs loan and security losses before depositors are harmed.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Bank capital K = (R + S + L) - (D + B) represents shareholders' residual claim and absorbs asset write-downs dollar-for-dollar so fixed depositor claims remain protected.

options_template.text: Vault cash plus deposits at the Federal Reserve; it is used to clear daily checks between banks.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Reserves-Capital Confusion): Vault cash plus Fed account balances define bank reserves (an asset), not bank capital (net worth).

options_template.text: Total customer deposits plus short-term borrowing; it measures the bank's total funding liabilities.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Liability-Equity Confusion): Customer deposits and short-term borrowing are liabilities owed to creditors, whereas bank capital is the residual equity cushion.

options_template.text: Total loans minus marketable securities; it measures how much credit the bank can still originate.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Asset-Difference Error): Subtracting securities from loans does not equal net worth and ignores reserves, deposits, and borrowing.

questions.title: Liquidity Risk vs. Credit (Insolvency) Risk
questions.prompt_template: How does liquidity risk differ from credit (insolvency) risk for a commercial bank?

hints.text: Ask whether a bank with positive net worth can still run out of immediately spendable cash.
Contrast an immediate shortage of reserves with asset values falling permanently below liabilities.

options_template.text: Liquidity risk occurs only during inflation, whereas insolvency risk occurs only during deflation.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Macro-Condition Confusion): Both risks depend on a bank's balance sheet structure and asset values, not exclusively on inflation versus deflation.

options_template.text: Liquidity risk means liabilities exceed assets, whereas insolvency risk means the bank lacks vault cash for one afternoon.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Definition Reversal): That reverses the two concepts: insolvency means liabilities exceed assets (negative capital), while illiquidity means lacking immediate cash/reserves.

options_template.text: Liquidity risk is the danger of lacking immediate cash or reserves to meet withdrawals even when solvent; insolvency risk is the danger that asset values fall below liabilities, wiping out capital.
options_template.feedback: Correct. An illiquid bank may hold sound long-term loans yet lack cash to meet sudden withdrawals, whereas an insolvent bank has negative net worth because its assets are worth less than its liabilities.

options_template.text: Liquidity risk applies only to credit unions, whereas insolvency risk applies only to large national banks.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Institutional Scope Error): All depository institutions engaging in maturity transformation face both liquidity risk and credit/insolvency risk.

questions.title: Structure of the Federal Reserve Board of Governors
questions.prompt_template: How is the Federal Reserve Board of Governors structured to insulate U.S. monetary policy from short-term political pressure?

hints.text: Recall how many Governors sit on the Board in Washington, D.C. and how long their terms last.
Remember that one Governor's term expires every two years.

options_template.text: Twelve Governors elected directly by voters every four years alongside the presidential election
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Governance Confusion): Governors are not popularly elected and there are 7 Governors (not 12); tying terms to presidential elections would increase political pressure.

options_template.text: Seven Governors nominated by the President and confirmed by the Senate, serving staggered 14-year non-renewable terms
options_template.feedback: Correct. Staggered 14-year terms (one expiring every two years) prevent any single presidential administration from packing the Board to engineer pre-election stimulus.

options_template.text: Five Governors appointed by commercial bank CEOs for lifetime tenure without Senate confirmation
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Private-Control Myth): The Board of Governors is a federal government agency whose 7 members are presidential nominees confirmed by the U.S. Senate.

options_template.text: Seven Governors appointed by the Secretary of the Treasury who serve at the pleasure of the President
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Executive-Control Error): Governors are independent statutory appointees with 14-year terms and cannot be removed simply over policy disagreements.

questions.title: Voting Composition of the FOMC
questions.prompt_template: Which combination of officials makes up the 12 voting members of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC)?

hints.text: Start with all members of the Board of Governors and add the permanent regional seat.
Remember that all 12 Regional Reserve Bank Presidents attend meetings, but only a subset vote in any given year.

options_template.text: All 12 Regional Federal Reserve Bank Presidents, with the Board of Governors serving only as non-voting advisors
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Governance Reversal): All 7 members of the Board of Governors hold permanent voting seats on the FOMC, not merely advisory roles.

options_template.text: The 7 members of the Board of Governors and 5 Senators from the Senate Banking Committee
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Branch-of-Government Confusion): Members of Congress do not sit or vote on the FOMC; the remaining 5 voting seats belong to Regional Reserve Bank Presidents.

options_template.text: The Fed Chair, the Treasury Secretary, and 10 rotating Regional Reserve Bank Presidents
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Treasury-Seat Error): The Secretary of the Treasury is not a member of the FOMC, and all 7 Board Governors vote.

options_template.text: All 7 members of the Board of Governors, the President of the New York Fed (permanent vote), and 4 of the remaining 11 Regional Bank Presidents rotating annually
options_template.feedback: Correct. The 12-member FOMC combines national public oversight (7 Governors) with regional representation (the New York Fed President permanently, plus 4 rotating regional presidents).

questions.title: Administered Rates in the Post-2020 Ample-Reserves Regime
questions.prompt_template: In the Federal Reserve's post-2020 ample-reserves operating regime, what is the role of Interest on Reserve Balances (IORB)?

hints.text: Recall which institutions hold reserve accounts directly at the Federal Reserve.
Distinguish the rate paid to banks on reserves from the rate offered to nonbank money market funds (ON RRP) and the borrowing rate at the Discount Window.

options_template.text: It is the administered interest rate the Fed pays depository institutions on reserves held at the Fed, anchoring banks' willingness to lend overnight.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because banks can earn IORB risk-free on their Fed reserve balances, IORB serves as the Fed's primary administered rate anchoring overnight interbank lending rates.

options_template.text: It is the penalty interest rate commercial banks must pay the Fed when they fail to meet a 10% required reserve ratio.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Pre-2020 Scarce-Reserves Myth): IORB is interest paid by the Fed to banks—not a penalty—and U.S. reserve requirements were reduced to 0% in March 2020.

options_template.text: It is the interest rate paid exclusively to nonbank money market mutual funds to establish a floor under overnight market rates.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Tool Confusion): The facility offering a safe administered rate to eligible nonbank financial institutions like money market funds is the ON RRP facility, not IORB.

options_template.text: It is the interest rate charged to sound banks when they borrow overnight reserves against collateral from the Discount Window.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Tool Confusion): Overnight collateralized borrowing from a Regional Federal Reserve Bank occurs at the Discount Window (Primary Credit Rate), not IORB.

questions.title: Transfer Between Checking and Savings Accounts (Post-May 2020)
questions.prompt_template: Using the nested post-May 2020 monetary aggregate diagram (M1 inside M2), what is the immediate effect on M1 and M2 when a household transfers $5,000 from its checking account to its household savings account?

hints.text: Locate both demand deposits (checking) and household savings deposits inside the post-May 2020 nested boxes.
If an asset moves between two items inside the same inner box, does the box total change?

options_template.text: M1 decreases by $5,000 and M2 remains unchanged.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Pre-May 2020 Classification Error): Under the outdated pre-2020 definition, savings accounts were outside M1; since May 2020, savings deposits are inside M1.

options_template.text: M1 decreases by $5,000 and M2 decreases by $5,000.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Aggregate Leakage Error): Moving funds between checking and savings does not remove money from the banking system; both balances remain inside M1 and M2.

options_template.text: Both M1 and M2 remain unchanged.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Under the post-May 2020 H.6 framework, demand deposits and household savings deposits (other liquid deposits) both lie inside the M1 inner box, so neither M1 nor M2 changes.

options_template.text: M1 increases by $5,000 and M2 remains unchanged.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sign Reversal): Checking accounts are already part of M1, so transferring out of checking into savings does not create new M1 balances.

questions.title: Moving Funds from Checking into a Small-Denomination CD
questions.prompt_template: In the nested monetary aggregate architecture (M1 inside M2), what happens to M1 and M2 when a household transfers $10,000 from its checking account into a 12-month retail Certificate of Deposit (CD)?

hints.text: Trace the $10,000 across the boundary between the inner M1 box and the outer M2 box.
Remember that CDs under $100,000 are small-denomination time deposits inside M2 but outside M1.

options_template.text: M1 decreases by $10,000, while M2 remains unchanged.
options_template.feedback: Correct. The $10,000 leaves the inner M1 box (demand deposits fall) and enters the M2-only ring (small time deposits rise by $10,000), leaving total M2 unchanged.

options_template.text: Both M1 and M2 decrease by $10,000.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Nested-Set Oversight): Because M2 includes small-denomination time deposits under $100,000, the $10,000 remains inside M2.

options_template.text: M1 remains unchanged, while M2 increases by $10,000.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Double-Counting Transfer): The funds were withdrawn from a checking account inside M1, so M1 must fall rather than stay unchanged.

options_template.text: Both M1 and M2 remain unchanged.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Liquidity Boundary Error): Small-denomination time deposits are not included in M1; only savings deposits and NOW accounts were grouped into M1's other liquid deposits.

questions.title: Depositing Currency from Your Wallet into Checking
questions.prompt_template: Suppose you deposit $2,000 of paper currency from your wallet into your checking account at a commercial bank. How does this transaction immediately affect M1 and M2?

hints.text: Check which two sub-components of M1 = C + DD + OLD change when cash moves from your wallet to your checking account.
Remember that currency inside the bank's vault is no longer counted in C.

options_template.text: M1 increases by $2,000 and M2 increases by $2,000.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Vault-Cash Double Counting): Counting both the new $2,000 checking deposit and the $2,000 cash now in the bank's vault double-counts the same money; C falls by $2,000 while DD rises by $2,000.

options_template.text: M1 decreases by $2,000 and M2 remains unchanged.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Currency-Only Fallacy): Demand deposits are also inside M1, so converting currency into a checking balance does not shrink M1.

options_template.text: M1 remains unchanged, while M2 increases by $2,000.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Subset Inconsistency): Because M1 is a subset of M2, a reallocation strictly inside M1 cannot change M2.

options_template.text: Both M1 and M2 remain unchanged.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Currency in circulation outside banks (C) falls by $2,000 and demand deposits (DD) rise by $2,000, leaving M1 = C + DD + OLD and M2 completely unchanged.

questions.title: Selling Corporate Stock into a Retail Money Market Fund
questions.prompt_template: In the nested monetary aggregate diagram, corporate stocks lie in the outer excluded universe. If an investor sells $25,000 of corporate stock to a brokerage dealer (paid from non-monetary institutional funds) and places the proceeds into a retail money market mutual fund, how do M1 and M2 change?

hints.text: Identify which box corporate stock starts in and which box retail money market mutual funds occupy.
Notice whether the funds ever enter the inner M1 box.

options_template.text: M1 increases by $25,000 and M2 increases by $25,000.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (M1 Boundary Error): Retail money market mutual fund shares are part of M2, not M1, so M1 does not rise.

options_template.text: M1 remains unchanged, while M2 increases by $25,000.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Moving $25,000 from an excluded non-monetary asset (equities) into a retail money market mutual fund adds $25,000 to the M2-only ring while leaving M1 unchanged.

options_template.text: Both M1 and M2 remain unchanged.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Asset-Equivalence Fallacy): Corporate stock is not part of M2, whereas retail money market mutual funds are included in M2.

options_template.text: M1 decreases by $25,000, while M2 increases by $25,000.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Wrong Source Account): The purchase of the retail money market fund was financed by selling stock outside M1, not by withdrawing from a checking account.

questions.title: Repaying Bank Loan Principal from a Checking Account
questions.prompt_template: Just as commercial bank loan origination creates new checkable deposits, what happens to a bank's T-account and to the M1 money supply when a business repays $30,000 of loan principal directly from its checking account at that bank?

hints.text: Trace the reverse of loan origination on both sides of the commercial bank's T-account.
Check what happens to customer checkable deposits (DD) when loan principal is extinguished.

options_template.text: Loans decrease by $30,000, checkable deposits decrease by $30,000, and M1 decreases by $30,000.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Repaying loan principal from a checking account shrinks both the bank's loan asset and its checkable deposit liability by $30,000, extinguishing $30,000 of M1 money.

options_template.text: Reserves increase by $30,000, loans decrease by $30,000, and M1 remains unchanged.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Cash-Vault Myth): Because the borrower pays from its checking account at the same bank rather than handing over outside currency, checkable deposits fall rather than reserves rising.

options_template.text: Bank capital increases by $30,000, loans decrease by $30,000, and M1 remains unchanged.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Principal-as-Profit Error): Repaying loan principal reduces both an asset (loans) and a liability (deposits) equally, leaving bank capital unchanged.

options_template.text: Loans decrease by $30,000, checkable deposits decrease by $30,000, and M1 increases by $30,000.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sign Reversal): A reduction in checkable deposits reduces M1; it does not increase M1.

questions.title: Immediate T-Account Effect of Originating a New Loan
questions.prompt_template: When a commercial bank approves a $50 million business loan and credits the borrower's checking account (before the borrower spends the funds), how does the bank's T-account change immediately?

hints.text: Remember that modern banks do not lend by handing out suitcases of vault cash.
Check which entry rises on the Assets side and which entry rises on the Liabilities & Capital side.

options_template.text: Reserves fall by $50M and Loans rise by $50M; Total Assets and M1 are unchanged.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Cash-Warehouse Fallacy): The bank does not immediately lose reserves when originating a loan; it creates a new checking deposit liability, expanding both Total Assets and M1.

options_template.text: Loans rise by $50M and Bank Capital rises by $50M; Total Liabilities are unchanged.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Equity-Creation Fallacy): Creating a loan creates a matching deposit liability owed to the borrower, not shareholder equity.

options_template.text: Loans rise by $50M on the Assets side and Checkable Deposits rise by $50M on the Liabilities side, expanding Total Assets and M1 by $50M.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Simultaneous accounting entries record the $50M loan asset and the $50M checkable deposit liability, expanding the bank's balance sheet and M1 immediately.

options_template.text: Securities fall by $50M and Checkable Deposits rise by $50M; Total Assets are unchanged.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Asset-Swap Error): Originating a loan adds to Loans rather than reducing Securities, and both sides of the T-account must rise by $50M to stay balanced.

questions.title: Interbank Settlement Outflow on a T-Account
questions.prompt_template: After a borrower receives a $50 million loan in her checking account at Bank A, she writes a $50 million check to a supplier who deposits it at Bank B. Once the Federal Reserve clears this payment, what is the change on Bank A's T-account?

hints.text: Trace how the Federal Reserve settles a check written from a Bank A depositor to a Bank B depositor.
Look for one Asset item and one Liability item at Bank A that both decline by $50 million.

options_template.text: Bank A's Loans fall by $50M and Checkable Deposits fall by $50M.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Loan-Disappearance Error): The borrower still owes Bank A the $50M loan; Bank A loses reserves to Bank B during clearing rather than losing the loan asset.

options_template.text: Bank A's Reserves fall by $50M and Checkable Deposits fall by $50M.
options_template.feedback: Correct. The Fed transfers $50M of reserves from Bank A's Fed account to Bank B's Fed account while Bank A debits the borrower's checking account by $50M.

options_template.text: Bank A's Reserves fall by $50M and Bank Capital falls by $50M.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Capital-Hit Error): A customer spending her own deposit reduces a liability (deposits) alongside an asset (reserves), leaving Bank A's capital unchanged.

options_template.text: Bank A's Checkable Deposits fall by $50M and Short-Term Borrowing rises by $50M automatically.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Automatic-Borrowing Assumption): Interbank clearing first draws down Bank A's reserves; borrowing is only needed if Bank A lacks sufficient reserves to cover the outflow.

questions.title: Balance Sheet Shift After a Loan Default Write-Off
questions.prompt_template: Suppose a commercial bank writes off $40 million in defaulted business loans as uncollectible. How does this write-off shift the bank's T-account?

hints.text: Ask whether depositors' legal balances shrink automatically when another borrower defaults.
Use the identity K = (R + S + L) - (D + B) to see which right-hand item absorbs the $40M asset drop.

options_template.text: Loans fall by $40M and Customer Deposits fall by $40M, leaving Bank Capital unchanged.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Depositor-Haircut Error): Customer deposits are fixed nominal promises; writing off a borrower's loan does not legally erase depositors' checking balances.

options_template.text: Loans fall by $40M and Reserves rise by $40M, leaving Total Assets unchanged.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Default-as-Repayment Error): A loan default destroys asset value rather than converting the loan into cash reserves.

options_template.text: Reserves fall by $40M and Bank Capital falls by $40M, leaving Loans unchanged.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Wrong Asset Entry): The write-off reduces the Loans asset on the left side of the T-account, not cash Reserves.

options_template.text: Loans fall by $40M on the Assets side and Bank Capital falls by $40M on the Liabilities & Capital side, while Deposits remain unchanged.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because deposits and borrowing are fixed obligations, any decline in asset value reduces Bank Capital dollar-for-dollar until capital reaches zero.

questions.title: T-Account Effect of Discount Window Borrowing During a Withdrawal
questions.prompt_template: A solvent bank holds $40M in reserves and faces an immediate $50M deposit withdrawal. It pledges Treasury securities as collateral at the Fed Discount Window to borrow $10M in reserves and pays all $50M to withdrawing depositors. Compared to its initial T-account, what is the net change after the withdrawal settles?

hints.text: Combine the two steps: first borrowing $10M (+R, +B), then paying out $50M (-R, -D).
Check whether Bank Capital K changes during a collateralized liquidity loan.

options_template.text: Reserves fall by $40M, Deposits fall by $50M, Borrowing rises by $10M, and Bank Capital is unchanged.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Total Assets decline by $40M (reserves drop from $40M to $0M), while on the right side Deposits drop by $50M and Borrowing rises by $10M (net -$40M), leaving Bank Capital untouched.

options_template.text: Reserves fall by $50M, Deposits fall by $50M, and Bank Capital falls by $10M.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Capital-Drain Error): Borrowing at the Discount Window creates a liability (B rises by $10M) rather than destroying equity capital, and reserves cannot fall below $0M.

options_template.text: Securities fall by $10M, Reserves fall by $40M, and Deposits fall by $50M.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Collateral-Sale Confusion): Pledging Treasury securities as collateral does not sell them; the bank retains ownership of the securities while recording a $10M Discount Window borrowing liability.

options_template.text: Reserves rise by $10M, Deposits fall by $50M, and Total Assets rise by $10M.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Incomplete Settlement): The $10M borrowed plus the $40M initial reserves are paid out to depositors, so ending reserves are $0M and Total Assets shrink by $40M.

questions.title: Distinguishing Reserves and Capital on Opposite Sides of the T-Account
questions.prompt_template: A commercial bank holds $150M in reserves (15% of its $1,000M in total assets) but only $15M in bank capital (1.5% of total assets). Based on the T-account structure, which vulnerability is most acute for this bank?

hints.text: Compare the size of the bank's liquidity cushion (Reserves) against its solvency cushion (Bank Capital).
Ask what happens if just 2% of its assets lose value.

options_template.text: Acute illiquidity risk, because its $15M in capital is too small to clear daily customer checks.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Reserves-Capital Inversion): Daily check clearing draws on Reserves ($150M), not Bank Capital ($15M).

options_template.text: Neither risk, because high reserves automatically guarantee high bank capital.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (False Equivalence): Reserves sit on the Asset side while Capital sits on the Equity side; a bank can hold ample cash reserves while being thinly capitalized.

options_template.text: Acute insolvency risk, because even a 2% decline in total asset value ($20M) would wipe out its $15M capital buffer despite abundant reserves.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Reserves protect against liquidity outflows, whereas Bank Capital absorbs asset losses; a $20M asset loss turns $15M of capital into -$5M (insolvency).

options_template.text: Insolvency risk is impossible as long as reserves exceed bank capital.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ratio Myth): Reserves exceeding capital does not prevent insolvency; solvency depends strictly on whether Total Assets exceed Total Liabilities (K > 0).

questions.title: Effect of Higher Bank Excess Reserves on the Generalized Money Multiplier
questions.prompt_template: In the generalized money multiplier equation m = (1 + c) / (rr + e + c), how does an increase in banks' voluntary excess reserve ratio (e) shift the relationship between the monetary base (MB) and M1?

hints.text: Check whether e appears in the numerator, the denominator, or both of m = (1 + c) / (rr + e + c).
Think about what happens to deposit creation when banks hold more reserves idle rather than lending them out.

options_template.text: The money multiplier m increases, amplifying the M1 expansion per dollar of base money.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Direction Reversal): Because e sits in the denominator, raising e strictly reduces m (dm/de < 0).

options_template.text: The money multiplier m decreases, weakening the link between an expansion in MB and M1.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Since dm/de = -(1 + c)/(rr + e + c)^2 < 0, higher voluntary excess reserves shrink the multiplier and decouple base money from M1.

options_template.text: The money multiplier m remains constant as long as the required reserve ratio rr is unchanged.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Simple-Multiplier Fallacy): Only the stylized 1/rr formula ignores excess reserves; in reality, higher voluntary reserve holdings reduce deposit multiplication.

options_template.text: The money multiplier m becomes negative whenever e exceeds rr.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sign Error): Because 1 + c > 0 and rr + e + c > 0, m remains strictly positive even when e > rr.

questions.title: Effect of a Higher Public Currency-Deposit Ratio (c)
questions.prompt_template: According to the generalized money multiplier m = (1 + c) / (rr + e + c), what happens to m if households decide to hold a larger fraction of their money as physical cash rather than bank deposits (c rises), assuming rr + e < 1?

hints.text: Notice that c increases both the numerator and the denominator by the same absolute amount, while initially (1 + c) > (rr + e + c).
Recall the economic intuition: cash held in wallets cannot be lent out by banks to create additional deposits.

options_template.text: The money multiplier m decreases, because currency held outside banks does not support multiple deposit creation.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Mathematically, dm/dc = (rr + e - 1)/(rr + e + c)^2 < 0 whenever rr + e < 1; economically, cash drains out of the banking system reduce deposit multiplication.

options_template.text: The money multiplier m increases, because c appears in the numerator (1 + c).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Numerator-Only Bias): Adding the same increment to both numerator and denominator of a fraction greater than 1 pulls the fraction downward toward 1, not upward.

options_template.text: The money multiplier m is completely unchanged because the +c terms in the numerator and denominator cancel out.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Algebraic Cancellation Error): Additive terms in a numerator and denominator do not cancel out; (1 + c)/(rr + e + c) is not equal to 1/(rr + e).

options_template.text: The money multiplier m drops immediately to zero as soon as c > 0.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Boundary Error): Even if households hold currency, m stays positive (and above 1 whenever rr + e < 1).

questions.title: Policy Transmission Flow in the Federal Reserve System
questions.prompt_template: In the institutional flowchart of the Federal Reserve System (Figure 11.3), how do policy decisions flow from Federal Reserve governance bodies to commercial banks and financial markets?

hints.text: Trace the arrows from the Board of Governors and the 12 Regional Reserve Banks into the FOMC and down to depository institutions.
Identify the post-2020 instruments shown on the transmission arrow from the FOMC to depository institutions.

options_template.text: Commercial banks elect the FOMC, which then instructs the Board of Governors to set required reserve ratios.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inverted Authority): Commercial banks do not elect the FOMC, and the Fed does not rely on changing required reserve ratios to steer rates.

options_template.text: The 12 Regional Banks independently set 12 separate federal funds rates for their own districts.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Fragmented-Policy Error): Monetary policy is unified nationally by the FOMC, which sets a single target range for the federal funds rate.

options_template.text: All 7 Board Governors and 5 voting Regional Presidents converge in the FOMC, which steers short-term rates through administered rates (IORB, ON RRP, Discount Rate).
options_template.feedback: Correct. The Board of Governors and Regional Banks converge in the 12-member FOMC, which implements monetary policy through administered rates and liquidity backstops.

options_template.text: The FOMC lends directly to households and businesses, bypassing commercial banks entirely.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Central-vs-Commercial Bank Confusion): The Fed conducts monetary policy and provides liquidity backstops through depository institutions and financial markets, not retail household lending.

questions.title: Counting Relative Prices in a Barter Economy
questions.prompt_template: A barter economy trades N = 200 distinct goods without using money. Using the bilateral exchange ratio formula N(N - 1)/2, how many relative prices must traders track compared to only 200 money prices in a monetary economy?

hints.text: Substitute N = 200 into the barter relative-price formula N(N - 1) / 2.
Compute 200 x 199 first, then divide by 2 so each pair of goods is counted once.

options_template.text: 40,000 relative prices
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Formula Error N^2): Computing N^2 = 200 x 200 includes trading each good for itself and double-counts every pair.

options_template.text: 19,900 relative prices
options_template.feedback: Correct. N(N - 1)/2 = 200(199)/2 = 100 x 199 = 19,900 bilateral exchange ratios, illustrating the massive transaction-cost savings of a unit of account.

options_template.text: 39,800 relative prices
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Missing Division by 2): Computing N(N - 1) = 200 x 199 = 39,800 double-counts each pair (both A-for-B and B-for-A).

options_template.text: 200 relative prices
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Monetary-Economy Confusion): 200 is the number of prices required when money serves as a unit of account, not under barter.

questions.title: Computing Post-May 2020 M1 from a Monetary Report
questions.prompt_template: A national monetary report lists the following balances (in billions of dollars): Currency in circulation outside banks = $2,100; Vault cash inside commercial banks = $85; Demand deposits = $4,800; Savings deposits & NOW accounts (other liquid deposits) = $9,600; Small-denomination time deposits (< $100,000) = $1,150; Retail money market mutual funds = $1,550; Unused credit card limits = $3,900. What is M1 under the post-May 2020 definition?

hints.text: Apply M1 = C + DD + OLD, remembering that post-May 2020 OLD includes household savings deposits.
Exclude bank vault cash, time deposits, retail money market funds, and credit card limits.

options_template.text: $16,500 billion
options_template.feedback: Correct. M1 = C ($2,100B) + DD ($4,800B) + OLD ($9,600B) = $16,500 billion. Vault cash, M2-only items, and credit lines are excluded.

options_template.text: $16,585 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Vault Cash Double Counting): Adding $85B of bank vault cash ($16,500B + $85B = $16,585B) double-counts cash held inside banks.

options_template.text: $6,900 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Pre-May 2020 Omission): Summing only C + DD ($2,100B + $4,800B = $6,900B) omits $9,600B of savings deposits and NOW accounts included in post-May 2020 M1.

options_template.text: $19,200 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (M1-M2 Confusion): Adding small time deposits ($1,150B) and retail money market funds ($1,550B) yields M2 ($19,200B), not M1.

questions.title: Computing Post-May 2020 M2 While Filtering Excluded Assets
questions.prompt_template: Suppose a monetary table reports (in billions of dollars): Currency in circulation = $2,300; Bank vault cash = $110; Demand deposits = $5,200; Savings deposits & NOW accounts = $10,500; Small-denomination time deposits (< $100,000) = $1,240; Retail money market mutual funds = $1,760; Large-denomination time deposits ($100,000 or more) = $2,400; Unused credit card limits = $4,100. What is M2?

hints.text: First compute M1 = C + DD + OLD, then add small-denomination time deposits and retail money market mutual funds.
Filter out vault cash, large time deposits ($100,000 or more), and unused credit card limits.

options_template.text: $23,400 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Large-CD Inclusion Error): Adding $2,400B of large-denomination institutional time deposits ($21,000B + $2,400B = $23,400B) overstates M2.

options_template.text: $21,110 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Vault Cash Double Counting): Adding $110B of bank vault cash ($21,000B + $110B = $21,110B) improperly includes reserves inside M2.

options_template.text: $21,000 billion
$25,100 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Credit-Limit Inclusion Error): Adding $4,100B of unused credit card limits ($21,000B + $4,100B = $25,100B) treats borrowing capacity as money.

questions.title: Calculating Bank Capital from a Balance Sheet
questions.prompt_template: A commercial bank reports the following balance sheet items (in millions of dollars): Reserves = $95; Marketable securities = $245; Loans = $560; Customer deposits = $740; Short-term borrowing = $70. What is the bank's capital (net worth)?

hints.text: Sum all three asset items (R + S + L) and sum both liability items (D + B).
Apply the residual identity K = (R + S + L) - (D + B).

options_template.text: $160 million
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted Borrowing Liability): Subtracting only deposits ($900M - $740M = $160M) ignores $70M of short-term borrowing.

options_template.text: $95 million
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Reserves-Capital Confusion): $95M is the bank's Reserves (an asset), not its Bank Capital (net worth).

options_template.text: $65 million
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted Reserves & Borrowing): Computing ($245M + $560M) - $740M = $65M omits both Reserves on the asset side and Short-Term Borrowing on the liability side.

options_template.text: $90 million
options_template.feedback: Correct. Total Assets = $95M + $245M + $560M = $900M; Total Liabilities = $740M + $70M = $810M; Bank Capital K = $900M - $810M = $90 million.

questions.title: Calculating a Bank's Capital Ratio
questions.prompt_template: Harbor Bank holds $80M in reserves, $220M in Treasury securities, and $500M in loans, funded by $640M in customer deposits, $64M in short-term borrowing, and $96M in bank capital. What is Harbor Bank's Tier 1 leverage (capital) ratio?

hints.text: Use the formula Capital Ratio = Bank Capital (K) / Total Assets.
Compute Total Assets = R + S + L = $80M + $220M + $500M first.

options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Reserves-as-Capital Error): Dividing Reserves ($80M) by Total Assets ($800M) gives the reserve-to-asset ratio (10.0%), not the capital ratio.
Correct. Total Assets = $80M + $220M + $500M = $800M, so Capital Ratio = $96M / $800M = 0.12 = 12.0%.
Diagnostic fallacy (Wrong Denominator): Dividing Bank Capital ($96M) by Customer Deposits ($640M) yields 15.0%, whereas the leverage ratio divides by Total Assets ($800M).
Diagnostic fallacy (Borrowing-as-Equity Error): Adding short-term borrowing ($64M) to capital ($96M) and dividing $160M by $800M wrongly treats debt as equity capital.

questions.title: Post-Default Bank Capital and New Capital Ratio
questions.prompt_template: Pacific Bank starts with Reserves = $60M, Securities = $140M, Loans = $350M (Total Assets = $550M), Deposits = $420M, Borrowing = $40M, and Bank Capital = $90M. If $50M of its loans default and are written off, what is Pacific Bank's new capital ratio?

hints.text: Reduce both Total Assets and Bank Capital by the $50M loan write-off.
Divide the new Bank Capital by the new Total Assets.

options_template.feedback: Correct. After the $50M write-off, Bank Capital falls from $90M to $40M and Total Assets fall from $550M to $500M. The new capital ratio is $40M / $500M = 8.0%.
Diagnostic fallacy (Unadjusted Capital Error): Dividing the original capital ($90M) by the new Total Assets ($500M) ignores that Bank Capital absorbs the $50M loan loss.
Diagnostic fallacy (Stale Denominator Error): Dividing the new capital ($40M) by the original Total Assets ($550M) ignores that Total Assets also fell by $50M.
Diagnostic fallacy (Loss-Ratio Confusion): Dividing the $50M loan loss by $500M measures the loss relative to remaining assets, not remaining Bank Capital.

questions.title: Maximum Asset Decline Before Insolvency
questions.prompt_template: A regional bank has $1,200M in Total Assets (including $100M in reserves), $1,020M in customer deposits, and $84M in short-term borrowing. What is the maximum percentage decline in total asset value the bank can absorb before becoming insolvent (K = $0)?

hints.text: First find Bank Capital K = Total Assets - (Deposits + Borrowing).
Express K as a percentage of Total Assets to find the maximum percentage drop before K hits zero.

options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted Borrowing Liability): Computing ($1,200M - $1,020M) / $1,200M = 15.0% ignores the $84M in short-term borrowing owed to creditors.
Diagnostic fallacy (Borrowing-Ratio Confusion): Dividing short-term borrowing ($84M) by Total Assets ($1,200M) gives 7.0%, which is not the bank's capital buffer.
Correct. Bank Capital K = $1,200M - ($1,020M + $84M) = $96M. Because asset losses reduce K dollar-for-dollar, the bank can absorb up to $96M / $1,200M = 8.0% before K hits zero.
Diagnostic fallacy (Reserves-as-Solvency Buffer): Dividing reserves ($100M) by Total Assets ($1,200M) gives 8.33%, confusing liquidity reserves with solvency capital.

questions.title: Computing the Theoretical Simple Deposit Multiplier Upper Bound
questions.prompt_template: Under classical textbook assumptions—a strictly binding required reserve ratio of rr = 8% (0.08), zero excess reserves (e = 0), and zero currency drain (c = 0)—what is the maximum theoretical deposit expansion from a $40 million injection of new reserves?

hints.text: Apply the stylized benchmark equation Delta D_max = (1 / rr) x Delta R.
Convert 8% to the decimal 0.08 before dividing.

options_template.text: $3.2 million
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Multiplication-Division Reversal): Multiplying $40M x 0.08 = $3.2M calculates required reserves on $40M rather than dividing by rr.

options_template.text: $50 million
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Decimal-Place Error): Dividing $40M by 0.80 instead of 0.08 yields $50M, off by a factor of 10.

options_template.text: $460 million
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Multiplier-Minus-One Error): Computing $40M x (1/0.08 - 1) = $460M subtracts the initial $40M, which is not the total maximum deposit expansion (1/rr) x Delta R.

options_template.text: $500 million
options_template.feedback: Correct. With rr = 0.08, the simple deposit multiplier is 1 / 0.08 = 12.5, so Delta D_max = 12.5 x $40 million = $500 million.

questions.title: Calculating the Monetary Base (MB)
questions.prompt_template: Suppose the U.S. economy has Currency in public circulation (C) = $2,200B, Commercial bank vault cash = $120B, Commercial bank reserve balances at the Fed = $3,180B, Demand deposits = $5,000B, and Savings deposits & NOW accounts = $10,000B. What is the Monetary Base (MB)?

hints.text: Recall that MB = C + R, where total bank reserves R equal vault cash plus bank deposit balances at the Federal Reserve.
Do not include commercial bank customer deposits (DD or OLD) in the central bank's monetary base.

options_template.text: $5,380 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted Vault Cash): Summing only C ($2,200B) + Fed reserve balances ($3,180B) = $5,380B omits the $120B of vault cash that is part of total bank reserves R.

options_template.text: $5,500 billion
options_template.feedback: Correct. Total reserves R = $120B (vault cash) + $3,180B (Fed balances) = $3,300B; therefore MB = C + R = $2,200B + $3,300B = $5,500 billion.

options_template.text: $17,200 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (M1-MB Confusion): Summing $2,200B + $5,000B + $10,000B = $17,200B computes M1 rather than the monetary base MB.

options_template.text: $10,500 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Customer-Deposit Inclusion): Adding $5,000B of demand deposits into MB ($5,500B + $5,000B = $10,500B) mixes commercial bank liabilities with central bank base money.

questions.title: Evaluating the Generalized Money Multiplier with Zero Required Reserves
questions.prompt_template: In a post-March 2020 ample-reserves environment where the required reserve ratio is rr = 0.00, banks voluntarily hold an excess reserve-to-deposit ratio of e = 0.25, and the public holds a currency-to-deposit ratio of c = 0.25, what is the value of the generalized money multiplier m = (1 + c) / (rr + e + c)?

hints.text: Substitute rr = 0.00, e = 0.25, and c = 0.25 directly into m = (1 + c) / (rr + e + c).
Simplify the numerator (1 + 0.25) and the denominator (0.00 + 0.25 + 0.25) before dividing.

options_template.feedback: Correct. m = (1 + 0.25) / (0.00 + 0.25 + 0.25) = 1.25 / 0.50 = 2.5. Even with rr = 0%, excess reserves and currency holdings keep the multiplier finite.
Diagnostic fallacy (Deposit-Multiplier Formula): Computing 1 / (0.00 + 0.25 + 0.25) = 2.0 omits the +c term in the numerator (giving the deposit multiplier D/MB rather than the M1 multiplier).
Diagnostic fallacy (Ignored Currency Drain): Computing 1 / 0.25 = 4.0 ignores the public's currency-deposit ratio c = 0.25.
Diagnostic fallacy (Denominator Omission): Computing 1.25 / 0.25 = 5.0 includes c in the numerator while forgetting to add c in the denominator.

questions.title: Discount Window Borrowing and Post-Withdrawal Capital Ratio
questions.prompt_template: Sierra Bank begins with Reserves = $50M, Securities = $150M, Loans = $350M (Total Assets = $550M), Deposits = $450M, Borrowing = $40M, and Bank Capital = $60M. Suppose uninsured depositors withdraw $75M immediately, and Sierra Bank pledges Treasury securities at the Fed Discount Window to borrow the exact reserve shortfall needed to cover the withdrawal. How much does Sierra Bank borrow at the Discount Window, and what is its capital ratio after the withdrawal settles?

hints.text: Find the immediate cash shortfall: Withdrawal ($75M) minus initial Reserves ($50M).
After paying all $75M out (leaving R = $0M), compute new Total Assets ($0 + $150M + $350M) and divide unchanged Bank Capital ($60M) by new Total Assets.

options_template.text: $75M borrowed; 12.0% capital ratio
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ignored Existing Reserves): Borrowing the entire $75M ignores the $50M in reserves Sierra Bank already holds to meet withdrawals.

options_template.text: $25M borrowed; 7.0% capital ratio
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Borrowing-as-Capital-Loss Error): Subtracting the $25M Discount Window loan from Bank Capital ($35M / $500M = 7.0%) wrongly treats collateralized borrowing as an equity loss.

options_template.text: $25M borrowed; 12.0% capital ratio
options_template.feedback: Correct. The reserve shortfall is $75M - $50M = $25M (Borrowing rises to $65M). After paying depositors, R = $0M, Total Assets = $500M, K remains $60M, and the capital ratio is $60M / $500M = 12.0%.

options_template.text: $25M borrowed; 10.91% capital ratio
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Stale Asset Denominator): Dividing $60M by the initial Total Assets ($550M) ignores that Total Assets shrank to $500M after reserves were paid out.

questions.title: Tracing Reserves and Deposits Across Loan Origination and Clearing
questions.prompt_template: Bay Area Bank starts with Reserves = $110M, Securities = $190M, Loans = $500M, Deposits = $700M, Borrowing = $20M, and Capital = $80M. First, it originates a $60M commercial loan by crediting the borrower's checking account. Next, the borrower writes a $45M check to a supplier who deposits it at another bank, and the Fed clears the check. What are Bay Area Bank's ending Reserves and ending Deposits?

hints.text: Step 1 (Loan origination): Loans rise by $60M and Deposits rise by $60M; Reserves do not change yet.
Step 2 (Interbank clearing): Reserves fall by $45M and Deposits fall by $45M.

options_template.text: Reserves = $50M; Deposits = $760M
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Loan-Outflow Confusion): Reducing reserves by the full $60M loan and failing to debit Deposits by $45M reverses which step affects reserves and omits check clearing.

options_template.text: Reserves = $110M; Deposits = $715M
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted Reserve Settlement): When a check clears to an external bank, the Fed deducts $45M from Bay Area Bank's reserves, so Reserves cannot remain $110M.

options_template.text: Reserves = $65M; Deposits = $655M
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted Loan Deposit): Subtracting $45M from the initial $700M deposits forgets that originating the $60M loan first increased Deposits to $760M.

options_template.text: Reserves = $65M; Deposits = $715M
options_template.feedback: Correct. Origination raises Deposits to $700M + $60M = $760M; clearing the $45M check reduces Reserves to $110M - $45M = $65M and Deposits to $760M - $45M = $715M.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Interpreting the May 2020 Jump in FRED Series M1SL
questions.prompt_template: A student plots FRED series M1SL and M2SL across 2020 and observes M1SL leaping from roughly $4.8 trillion in April 2020 to over $16.2 trillion in May 2020, while M2SL rises smoothly with no vertical discontinuity. What is the correct empirical explanation?

hints.text: Recall what happened to Regulation D's six-per-month transfer limit on household savings accounts in spring 2020.
Ask why M2SL did not experience the same artificial jump as M1SL.

options_template.text: The Federal Reserve printed over $11 trillion in physical paper currency during May 2020 to fund pandemic relief.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Money-Printing Misreading): No overnight tripling of cash occurred; the jump reflects a statistical reclassification of existing savings deposits.

options_template.text: After suspending Regulation D's six-transfer limit on savings accounts, the Fed reclassified existing savings deposits from M2-only into M1, leaving M2 unaffected.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because savings deposits were already inside M2SL, moving them into M1SL created a massive definitional break in M1SL without causing any discontinuity in M2SL.

options_template.text: Commercial banks converted $11 trillion of corporate stocks into checking accounts in a single month.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Asset-Liquidation Myth): Equities were not liquidated into checking accounts; existing household savings accounts were simply redefined as part of M1.

options_template.text: Households paid off $11 trillion in credit card debt, which automatically added $11 trillion to M1SL.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Debt-Creation Reversal): Paying off credit card debt from checking reduces M1 rather than increasing it, and the May 2020 jump was a Regulation D reclassification.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Avoiding Measurement Traps When Analyzing M1SL Across 2020
questions.prompt_template: An analyst calculates the 12-month percentage growth rate of FRED's M1SL from January 2020 to January 2021 and concludes that U.S. spendable liquidity more than tripled due to reckless money creation. Why is this empirical conclusion flawed, and what is the better approach?

hints.text: Think about whether M1SL measured the exact same basket of accounts in January 2020 and January 2021.
Consider which FRED monetary aggregate remained definitionally consistent across May 2020.

options_template.text: The conclusion is flawed because M1SL is not seasonally adjusted; the analyst should simply use unadjusted M1 instead.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Seasonal-Adjustment Distractor): M1SL is already seasonally adjusted ('SL'); the distortion comes from the May 2020 definitional break, not seasonality.

options_template.text: The conclusion is flawed because M1SL excludes currency in circulation; the analyst should add bank vault cash.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Definition Error): M1SL includes currency in circulation and intentionally excludes vault cash to avoid double counting.

options_template.text: The conclusion is flawed because M1SL underwent a definitional break in May 2020; researchers should account for the reclassification or examine M2SL for consistent cross-2020 comparisons.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Comparing pre-May 2020 M1SL (excluding savings) with post-May 2020 M1SL (including savings) mixes two different definitions, whereas M2SL included savings both before and after May 2020.

options_template.text: The conclusion is completely valid because Federal Reserve statistical series are never affected by regulatory changes.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Data-Blindness Fallacy): Regulatory changes like lifting Regulation D's transfer cap can alter monetary aggregate definitions and create structural breaks in time-series data.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Diagnosing the March 2023 Collapse of Silicon Valley Bank
questions.prompt_template: In March 2023, Silicon Valley Bank (SVB) collapsed in less than 48 hours despite holding large portfolios of low-default-risk U.S. Treasury and agency bonds. Which combination of factors explains how this failure occurred?

hints.text: Recall how rising interest rates in 2022 affected the market value of long-term fixed-rate bonds.
Consider why SVB's corporate tech depositors rushed to withdraw $42 billion in a single day.

options_template.text: Sharp interest-rate hikes depressed the market value of SVB's long-term bonds, and uninsured depositors exceeding the $250,000 FDIC cap triggered a $42 billion run that forced capital-wiping fire sales.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Interest-rate risk created unrealized bond losses, and concentrated uninsured tech deposits sparked an acute liquidity run that forced SVB to realize losses exceeding its equity capital.

options_template.text: The Federal Reserve raised required reserve ratios to 25%, making it illegal for SVB to pay out customer deposits.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Policy-Fact Error): Reserve requirements remained at 0% after March 2020; SVB failed due to interest-rate risk, uninsured deposit flight, and realized bond losses.

options_template.text: SVB's borrowers defaulted on 90% of its residential mortgages during a single weekend.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Default-Only Myth): SVB's crisis was driven by falling market values on long-term Treasury/agency securities and an uninsured deposit run, not mass mortgage defaults.

options_template.text: FDIC insurance had been repealed in 2022, leaving retail households with $0 protection on small checking accounts.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Institutional Fact Error): FDIC insurance remained intact at $250,000 per depositor, per bank, per ownership category; SVB's vulnerability was its heavy reliance on uninsured balances above that cap.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Why Default-Free Bonds Can Still Endanger a Bank
questions.prompt_template: A bank executive argues: 'Our bank invests customer deposits exclusively in 20-year U.S. Treasury bonds. Because the U.S. government does not default on Treasury debt, our bank faces zero risk of failure.' Why is this argument dangerously incomplete?

hints.text: Separate credit (default) risk from interest-rate risk and liquidity risk.
Ask what happens to the market price of an existing 20-year fixed-rate bond when market interest rates rise sharply.

options_template.text: Because 20-year Treasury bonds are counted in M1, the Fed can cancel them whenever inflation rises.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Aggregate & Policy Error): Treasury bonds are excluded from M1 and M2, and the Fed does not cancel Treasury debt.

options_template.text: Because Treasury bonds are liabilities rather than assets on a commercial bank's balance sheet.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Balance-Sheet Error): Treasury securities are assets (S) on a bank's balance sheet, not liabilities.

options_template.text: Because FDIC insurance prohibits commercial banks from holding any U.S. Treasury securities.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Regulatory Myth): Banks routinely hold Treasury securities as High-Quality Liquid Assets; the danger is unhedged duration mismatch.

options_template.text: Even default-free long-term fixed-rate bonds lose market value when interest rates rise; if depositors run, forced sales realize those losses and can wipe out bank capital.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Maturity transformation exposes a bank holding long-duration fixed-rate bonds to severe interest-rate risk, which a sudden liquidity run can convert into realized insolvency.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Modern Lending Constraints vs. Simple Multiplier
questions.title: Why Zero Reserve Requirements Did Not Cause Infinite Money Creation
questions.prompt_template: In March 2020, the Federal Reserve reduced required reserve ratios to 0%. If a student applies the classical simple deposit multiplier (1/rr), the formula divides by zero and predicts infinite deposit creation. Why does commercial bank lending remain strictly finite in the real-world U.S. economy?

hints.text: Think about what constraints still bind a bank even when rr = 0%.
Recall the three real-world limits on commercial bank lending: capital adequacy, liquidity clearing buffers, and borrower demand.

options_template.text: Because commercial banks are legally barred from creating checkable deposits when originating loans.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Intermediation Myth): Commercial banks still create checkable deposits whenever they originate loans; lending is bounded by balance-sheet and market constraints, not a legal ban.

options_template.text: Because bank lending is constrained by regulatory capital adequacy ratios, liquidity buffers needed for interbank clearing, and creditworthy borrower demand at prevailing interest rates.
options_template.feedback: Correct. In an ample-reserves regime with rr = 0%, equity capital requirements, interbank settlement liquidity, and underwriting/credit demand—not a mechanical reserve ratio—bound deposit creation.

options_template.text: Because the U.S. returned to a gold standard in March 2020, capping M1 at physical gold holdings.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Gold-Standard Myth): The U.S. operates a pure fiat monetary system and did not return to a gold standard.

options_template.text: Because banks immediately transfer 100% of all new loans to the U.S. Treasury.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Institutional Error): Commercial banks retain loans as assets on their own balance sheets and do not transfer them to the Treasury.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Economic Rationale for Federal Reserve Political Insulation
questions.prompt_template: Why did Congress design the Federal Reserve with 14-year staggered Board terms and a hybrid FOMC combining Washington Governors with Regional Reserve Bank Presidents?

hints.text: Consider the short-term political temptation facing elected officials just before an election.
Think about what regional Federal Reserve Banks contribute to national monetary deliberations.

options_template.text: To prevent the Federal Reserve from ever lowering interest rates during a recession.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Mandate Distortion): The Fed actively lowers interest rates during recessions; independence protects long-run price stability rather than banning countercyclical policy.

options_template.text: To ensure that Congress directly votes on every change to the federal funds rate.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Governance Confusion): Congress sets the Fed's statutory mandate and conducts oversight, while delegating operational rate decisions to the independent FOMC.

options_template.text: To insulate monetary policy from short-term electoral pressure to engineer pre-election inflation while blending national oversight with decentralized regional economic intelligence.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Staggered 14-year terms curb short-term political manipulation, and Regional Bank Presidents bring grassroots district data (such as the Beige Book) into national policy debates.

options_template.text: To guarantee that commercial bank shareholders maximize profits without regulatory supervision.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Mission Confusion): The Federal Reserve is a public-purpose central bank tasked with macroeconomic stability and bank supervision, not commercial profit maximization.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Why the Discount Window Solves Illiquidity but Not Insolvency
questions.prompt_template: Suppose Bank X has positive capital ($60M) but lacks cash to meet a sudden $50M withdrawal, whereas Bank Y has negative capital (-$40M) after massive loan defaults. Why is Discount Window lending appropriate for Bank X but insufficient to cure Bank Y?

hints.text: Remember what Discount Window borrowing does to Assets, Liabilities, and Bank Capital (K).
Ask whether borrowing against collateral can turn negative net worth back into positive net worth.

options_template.text: Discount Window loans bridge temporary liquidity shortfalls against sound collateral without altering capital (K), whereas insolvent Bank Y requires equity recapitalization or FDIC resolution.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Borrowing reserves increases both Reserves (+R) and Borrowing (+B), leaving Bank Capital K unchanged; it prevents fire sales at solvent Bank X but cannot restore negative capital at Bank Y.

options_template.text: Discount Window loans automatically forgive a bank's loan losses, so Bank Y would become solvent while Bank X does not qualify.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Bailout Myth): The Discount Window provides collateralized overnight loans to sound depository institutions—not free equity grants that erase loan defaults.

options_template.text: Neither bank can use the Discount Window because the Fed abolished the Discount Window when moving to an ample-reserves regime.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Regime Fact Error): The Discount Window (Primary Credit Rate) remains an active pillar of the post-2020 ample-reserves framework and lender-of-last-resort backstop.

options_template.text: Bank Y is the better candidate for Discount Window lending because insolvent banks hold more unencumbered collateral than solvent banks.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Collateral Inversion): Insolvent banks have impaired assets worth less than their liabilities and lack the sound collateral required for standard lender-of-last-resort lending.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: How the Three Pillars of Banking Stability Reinforce One Another
questions.prompt_template: How do FDIC deposit insurance, prudential capital/liquidity supervision, and the Fed's Discount Window complement one another to prevent systemic banking panics?

hints.text: Match each pillar to the specific problem it addresses: retail panic, loss absorption/risk-taking, and sudden cash outflows.
Check why relying on only one pillar without the others leaves gaps.

options_template.text: All three pillars perform the exact same function of guaranteeing 100% of commercial bank shareholder stock prices.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Shareholder-Protection Myth): None of the pillars guarantee bank shareholders against losses; shareholders absorb losses first through bank capital.

options_template.text: FDIC insurance eliminates the need for bank capital, while the Discount Window eliminates the need for bank supervision.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Substitute Fallacy): Without capital and liquidity supervision, insured banks could take excessive risks; the three pillars are complements, not substitutes.

options_template.text: They work by forcing commercial banks to hold 100% of deposits as physical vault cash at all times.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (100%-Reserve Myth): Modern banking relies on maturity transformation and fractional liquidity buffers, not 100% vault cash.

options_template.text: FDIC insurance calms retail depositors, capital and liquidity rules ensure buffers absorb losses and limit excessive risk, and the Discount Window supplies emergency liquidity to solvent banks.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Together, the three pillars curb self-fulfilling retail runs, enforce loss-absorbing equity and liquid asset buffers, and prevent fire-sale contagion during liquidity squeezes.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Comparing Run Vulnerability: Diversified Retail vs. Concentrated Uninsured Deposits
questions.prompt_template: Bank Alpha and Bank Beta have identical total deposits of $10 billion. Bank Alpha's deposits come from 200,000 households averaging $50,000 each, whereas Bank Beta's deposits come from 500 tech startups averaging $20 million each. If negative rumors circulate about both banks, why does Bank Beta face a far greater risk of a rapid deposit run?

hints.text: Compare each bank's typical account size against the $250,000 FDIC deposit insurance limit.
Ask which set of depositors faces immediate loss exposure if the bank is closed.

options_template.text: Because Bank Alpha's retail depositors can withdraw cash faster than corporate treasurers using wire transfers.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Withdrawal-Speed Inversion): Corporate treasurers can move tens of millions electronically in minutes, and Bank Alpha's accounts are fully insured.

options_template.text: Because Bank Alpha's accounts fall well within the $250,000 FDIC insurance cap, whereas nearly all of Bank Beta's $20 million accounts are uninsured and have a strong incentive to flee first.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Fully insured retail depositors have little reason to panic, whereas uninsured corporate depositors above $250,000 face direct loss risk and have a powerful first-mover incentive to withdraw.

options_template.text: Because FDIC insurance covers only corporate startup accounts and excludes household checking accounts.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Coverage Reversal): FDIC insurance covers up to $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category—protecting small retail balances fully while leaving multi-million-dollar balances mostly uninsured.

options_template.text: Because Bank Alpha's deposits are excluded from M1 while Bank Beta's deposits are counted in M2.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Aggregate Irrelevance): Both banks' checking and savings deposits are part of M1; run vulnerability stems from uninsured deposit concentration, not M1/M2 classification.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Why the Fed Needs Both IORB and the ON RRP Facility
