questions.prompt_template: In the post-2020 ample-reserves operating regime, why does the Federal Reserve maintain the Overnight Reverse Repurchase Agreement (ON RRP) facility alongside Interest on Reserve Balances (IORB)?

hints.text: Recall which financial institutions are legally eligible to earn IORB and which major money-market lenders are not.
Think about what could happen to overnight market interest rates if nonbank lenders had no safe administered floor.

options_template.text: Because IORB applies only during recessions while ON RRP applies only during economic booms.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Regime-Splitting Error): Both IORB and ON RRP operate continuously together in the ample-reserves framework across all phases of the business cycle.

options_template.text: Because IORB sets the ceiling on overnight rates while ON RRP lends emergency funds to insolvent banks.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Tool-Role Confusion): The Discount Window (Primary Credit Rate) acts as the upper ceiling and emergency backstop, whereas ON RRP is a floor tool for nonbanks.

options_template.text: Because nonbank institutions like money market mutual funds cannot earn IORB; ON RRP offers them a safe administered rate, reinforcing a firm floor under short-term market rates.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Only depository institutions hold reserve accounts earning IORB; offering ON RRP to eligible nonbanks prevents short-term market rates from trading far below the FOMC's target range.

options_template.text: Because ON RRP directly sets 30-year fixed mortgage rates for retail homebuyers.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Term-Structure Confusion): ON RRP is an overnight administered facility anchoring short-term money-market rates, not a direct control on 30-year mortgage rates.

questions.topic: Base Money vs. Commercial Bank Deposit Creation
questions.title: Distinguishing Central Bank Base Money from Commercial Bank M1 Creation
questions.prompt_template: During an economic expansion, commercial banks approve $200 billion in new business loans while the Federal Reserve keeps the monetary base (MB = C + R) completely unchanged. What happens to M1 and MB, and what does this reveal about modern money creation?

hints.text: Recall who creates checkable deposits (inside M1) versus who creates base money (MB = C + R).
Verify whether commercial bank loan origination changes the Federal Reserve's balance sheet.

options_template.text: M1 rises by $200 billion while MB remains unchanged, showing that commercial banks create spendable checkable deposits independently of one-for-one changes in base money.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Loan origination creates new checkable deposits (expanding M1) without altering the Fed's monetary base, demonstrating why M1 and MB do not move in a rigid mechanical ratio.

options_template.text: Both M1 and MB rise by $200 billion, because commercial banks print new central bank reserves whenever they approve a loan.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Issuer Confusion): Commercial banks cannot create central bank reserves or currency; only the Federal Reserve can expand the monetary base MB.

options_template.text: Neither M1 nor MB changes, because commercial bank lending merely redistributes existing vault cash from savers to borrowers.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Loanable-Warehouse Fallacy): Commercial banks create new checkable deposits by expanding both loans and deposit liabilities, rather than handing out pre-existing vault cash.

options_template.text: MB falls by $200 billion while M1 rises by $200 billion, because lending permanently destroys central bank reserves.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Reserve-Destruction Error): Originating loans creates deposit liabilities and may redistribute reserves across banks during clearing, but it does not destroy aggregate system reserves.

questions.topic: Commodity Money vs. Fiat Money Policy Trade-Offs
questions.title: Macroeconomic Trade-Offs of Returning to a Gold Standard
questions.prompt_template: A commentator proposes abolishing fiat money and returning the United States to a strict gold commodity standard. Based on Chapter 11's analysis of commodity money, fiat money, and central banking, what is the core macroeconomic trade-off of this proposal?

hints.text: Identify the one historical advantage of commodity money regarding government over-issuance.
Contrast that advantage with the costs of tying the money supply to physical gold mining and restricting lender-of-last-resort flexibility.

options_template.text: A gold standard eliminates all banking crises and liquidity runs while allowing unlimited Discount Window lending.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Historical & Mechanical Error): Gold standards historically experienced frequent banking panics and severely constrained a central bank's ability to supply emergency liquidity.

options_template.text: A gold standard converts credit cards into M1 money and eliminates the need for commercial bank capital.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Unrelated Mechanisms): Backing currency with gold does not turn credit lines into money or eliminate credit/insolvency risk on bank balance sheets.

options_template.text: A gold standard guarantees higher economic growth because gold has zero storage or transportation costs.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Transaction-Cost Reversal): Commodity money is heavy to transport and costly to assay, which is why modern economies adopted fiat currency.

options_template.text: While gold naturally limits discretionary over-issuance, it is costly to transport, ties the money supply to mining discoveries, and restricts the central bank's lender-of-last-resort flexibility during crises.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Commodity money checks arbitrary money creation, but at the cost of tying macroeconomic liquidity to physical mining supply and handicapping emergency crisis stabilization.
